extracted.intended_audience: writers aspiring to write young adult (YA) novels / authors targeting teen readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for crafting young-adult (YA) novels that resonate with readers aged ~12–18, covering voice, themes, content, market research, and craft decisions specific to YA. Focuses on what makes a book ‘YA’ and concrete tips for authenticity and publication readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience: readers aged 12–18
rubrics_metrics.description: Young adult fiction is written for an audience of twelve to eighteen-year-olds, with more mature content geared towards the older readers in this age bracket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the intended age-range (12–18) in mind when choosing content maturity, language, and themes. While adults may enjoy YA, the book should speak primarily to teenage experience and concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must be a teenager / write from inside a teen's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: YA novels differ from adult novels in that a teenage character is the protagonist. Whatever is happening in the YA novel is happening to the teenager experiencing life as a teenager. YA fiction is not written with the hindsight of an adult looking back on their teenage years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narratorial hindsight or adult retrospection; the story must reflect a teen's present perspective and lack of adult-earned wisdom. Voice and choices should feel authentic to someone who hasn't yet lived through adulthood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical length guideline (50,000–75,000 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: In length, young adult books might vary anywhere from 50,000 - 75,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this range as a rough target when planning novel scope; some subgenres may deviate, but aim for this general length when preparing submissions or estimating pacing and plot complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher maturity allowance than middle-grade
rubrics_metrics.description: YA fiction deals with subject matter and themes that are more mature than those found in middle-grade fiction. While middle-grade might hint at romance or a first crush, YA might include more mature physical or emotional relationships and may include graphic violence, profanity, or sex not found in middle-grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how explicitly to depict mature content based on target age within YA (younger vs older teens) and the story's needs. Be intentional about inclusion of violence, sex, or profanity—use it to serve plot/character, not gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common YA themes (coming-of-age, first love, self-discovery, life & death, individuality, relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most YA novels will have common themes regardless of genre: coming of age, first love, self-discovery, life and death, individuality, relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose themes that are relevant to teen experience. Examples (The Fault in Our Stars, Six of Crows, The Giver) demonstrate that very different premises can all center on self-discovery, love, and grief. Make the theme central and resonant for your intended teen readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: YA is genre-flexible but must maintain YA perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: YA is not itself a genre of fiction; YA novels exist in all genres (romance, fantasy, historical, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can write YA in any genre, but ensure YA-specific concerns—teen protagonist, voice, thematics—remain central even when genre conventions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing is off-limits—handle sensitive subjects responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to subject matter in YA fiction, nothing is off-limits. Teens face many challenges, and YA can explore sensitive topics such as police violence, poverty, domestic abuse, racism, and suicide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tackle difficult subjects to allow teen readers to relate or learn about experiences beyond their own, but do so thoughtfully and responsibly. Use examples like The Hate U Give, Monday’s Not Coming, and Thirteen Reasons Why to see how heavy topics are handled; consider trigger warnings, sensitivity readers, and the impact on readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and authentic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary YA increasingly represents different gender identities and sexual orientations, enabling teens to find fiction to which they can relate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include diverse characters and relationships (e.g., same-sex or transgender couples) authentically. Representation should feel lived-in and specific rather than tokenistic; seek input from people with lived experience as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chasing fleeting trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't try to keep up with quickly moving trends. Publishing is a long game and a topic, musician, slang, or event trending now may be old news by publication time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on timeless emotional truths and strong storytelling rather than topical references that will date the book. If you do include contemporary details, ensure the story's core doesn't hinge on ephemeral trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid preachiness—prioritize compelling narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: While it's timeless to impart wisdom, be cautious about being preachy. Most YA novels avoid overt lectures; directness risks alienating young readers and having your book end up in their DNF pile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show character growth and themes through plot and emotional arc rather than explicit moralizing. Let readers draw conclusions through character choices and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read recent bestselling YA to understand market and reader response
rubrics_metrics.description: Read bestselling YA books published in the last five years to better understand what is selling and what readers are responding to. You can’t rely on books that were your favorites a decade ago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a reading spreadsheet tracking title, author, publisher, publication date, and—if useful—agents/editors (found in acknowledgments). This helps identify current market tastes and potential submission targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and understand teen culture (talk to teens, use social media like TikTok)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to write for young adults, you need to understand young adults. Talk to teens in your life, volunteer at schools/libraries, or research them through social media platforms such as TikTok.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find TikTokers or other creators who represent your ideal reader and take notes on language, interests, and concerns. Direct observation or conversations with teens will help avoid being out of touch and improve authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonists' concerns should extend beyond immediate circle
rubrics_metrics.description: While middle-grade protagonists tend to focus on friends, family, and their immediate world, YA protagonists are often trying to figure out their place in the greater world outside their immediate circle of family and friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the plot and character arc around the teen's movement toward autonomy, identity, or a larger role in society. Emphasize stakes that reflect growing awareness of the broader world rather than only local concerns.
